narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile of your cohort, far below the average ranking of accepted students (around the middle of the class), signaled to the model that you may struggle with the demands of bar preparation. Your first-year ranking, also in the bottom decile compared with an average of 6 among accepted applicants, added further weight in the same direction.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 worked in your favor. It sits noticeably above the 3.23 average of students who were admitted, and this stronger performance pulled the prediction back toward success. However, it was not enough to overcome the negative influence of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 29, well below the 37 average of accepted students, your middle-income background, full-time study plans, gender, and race played smaller roles; none of these protected characteristics were used by the model.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic standing if you retake courses, consider a structured bar-prep program that targets your specific weaknesses, and retake the LSAT if possible. Strengthening these academic signals will be the most direct way to change future model predictions in your favor. (248 words)
